rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form ʿamma represents ʿammā: ordinary speech suppresses the alif sound, and the spelling preserves that suppression.
rows.anchor: the sound of alif has been suppressed and the word is always written thus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word tasā’ul means people mutually asking one another about something.
rows.anchor: means to mutually ask one another about something.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An inquiry may seek research or information, but this one is ridicule and frivolous talk.
rows.anchor: it is merely to make fun and indulge in frivolous talk.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh tried to shield the public from the warnings because the sūrahs spread through their forceful tone and arguments.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh employed various foolish measures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mockers objected that people whose bones decayed or ancestors whose graves vanished could not be raised, and some emphatically denied resurrection.
rows.anchor: Some of them would ask how people can be re-created when their bones decay.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ridiculed Hell and the report that nineteen angels guard it, boasting they could defeat the guards.
rows.anchor: When the Qur’ ān informed them that nineteen angels guard Hell, they again started mocking this information.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran calls these remarks mutual questioning; its opening question signals that the warnings deserve fear and regret rather than amusement.
rows.anchor: what they are making fun of is not something to mock and made fun of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interrogative particle is omitted before the statement, a Quranic rhetorical ellipsis; 93:1–2 supplies an example, and exegetes who miss the style lose its force.
rows.anchor: Most of our exegetes are unaware of this style

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied question asks whether people dare mock the great news of resurrection, judgment, reward, and punishment, which should alarm them deeply.
rows.anchor: The meaning conveyed by the verse is:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtilāf conveys both disagreement and contradiction, since contradictory opinions generate differences; Islahi discusses this at 27:66.
rows.anchor: simultaneously expresses two meanings: firstly, difference in opinion and secondly, a contradiction in opinion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters split between outright denial and a majority who objected, doubting resurrection, expecting deities to rescue them, questioning universal accounting, and treating worldly prosperity as divine favor.
rows.anchor: a group among them would blatantly deny it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They held some truths that contradicted their errors but refused to examine inconsistencies despite reminders; reason required listening because the stakes were eternal.
rows.anchor: For this very reason, they were not ready to assess

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated warning says their comforting expectations will fail and accounts for both the worldly punishment of messenger-deniers and the punishment of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This is a very powerful warning to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Created signs display God’s power, providence, mercy, wisdom, and oneness; reflection on them leads to certainty that judgment has a fixed time.
rows.anchor: So manifest and palpable are these signs that no upright person can deny them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth is a comfortable cradle and mountains are fixed as pegs to stabilize it.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has made this earth a place of comfort for him much like a cradle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains balance the earth; providence entails accountability, since otherwise grateful and ungrateful people would be alike to the Creator.
rows.anchor: Providence always entails accountability. If this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “created you in pairs” is grammatically a statement, its coordination with the preceding question makes it interrogative in force.
rows.anchor: is a statement; however, in reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pairing comforts humanity: apparent opposites complement one another and spouses provide comfort and mental peace.
rows.anchor: Man was not created alone; he was provided with a mate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accord of spouses is a sign of divine oneness and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: as an argument for taw ḥīd and the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibāt literally means cutting off; here sleep also connotes relief from hardship and comfort.
rows.anchor: relief from hardship and comfort.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep interrupts continuous activity, relieves hardship, and restores the limbs through rest.
rows.anchor: breaks the continuous process of movement and action

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is like clothing because it conceals and protects people and gives rest and strength for renewed activity.
rows.anchor: the night has been made an apparel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Day is made a time to work for one’s livelihood.
rows.anchor: efforts to earn a livelihood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day are neither autonomous nor purposeless: God arranged them for human service, inviting gratitude and accountability.
rows.anchor: There obviously is a purpose in directing our attention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After earthly signs, the discourse turns to the sky; seven sturdy heavens are like the layered, flawless heavens in 67:3–4.
rows.anchor: the attributes mentioned clearly indicate that it is the sky

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boundless sky is sound and flawless wherever one looks.
rows.anchor: find it absolutely sound and flawless.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lamp is the sun, source of worldly light, heat, and power; harmony between sky and earth shows one God governs both.
rows.anchor: source of light, heat and power.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muʿṣirāt describes water-laden clouds or clouds producing rain, with no essential difference between these senses.
rows.anchor: clouds replete with water and also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Māʾ thajjāj means pounding, widespread, continuous rain; rain displays sky–earth harmony and supports monotheism, providence, and accountability.
rows.anchor: pounding, widespread and continuous rain.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain produces grain for people, grass and vegetation for cattle, and luxuriant orchards.
rows.anchor: provide grain for man and grass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed Judgment sums up the argument: the provider gathers humanity, judges who recognized or ignored His favors, and rewards or punishes them.
rows.anchor: the Almighty Who has done all this will not leave man unaccountable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement of judgment after the signs shows that the world’s system proclaims that day; sun, moon, clouds, and winds serve human needs.
rows.anchor: The sun, the moon, the clouds and the winds and other phenomena are put in the service of man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After arguments for judgment, the passage portrays cosmic upheaval and the fate of the rebellious and disobedient.
rows.anchor: these verses portray the upheaval which will take place in the universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the trumpet, resurrection is effortless for God: people emerge from graves in crowds and head to the caller; elsewhere they are likened to locusts.
rows.anchor: At the sound of a trumpet, people will come out from their graves in multitudes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparently solid, uncracked dome of sky opens so that gates appear everywhere.
rows.anchor: this sky which today seems to be so strong and robust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The firmly set mountains move and become fragile like sand dunes.
rows.anchor: they will be fragile like dunes of sand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell appears immediately after the upheaval as though it had lain in ambush; rebels get no time to prepare.
rows.anchor: Hell will appear so suddenly as if it was lying in ambush

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret ahqāb as a long but finite period, implying that Hell eventually ends.
rows.anchor: Hell will come to an end one day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the finite-period view: concise ahqāb must be read by the comprehensive promise of everlasting residence, and elsewhere the rebellious never leave Hell.
rows.anchor: interpret the concise in the light of the comprehensive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned get nothing cool; lexicographers explain ghassāq as blood and pus, boiling-hot water, or dirty water, while al-Mursalāt’s shade is smoke that offers no relief.
rows.anchor: explained by lexicographers as blood and pus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment corresponds to deeds: each good or evil deed yields its own outcome in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: good or evil deed will bear result as per its nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Offenders never feared accountability and recklessly denied revealed signs; the verbal noun kidhdhāban intensifies denial.
rows.anchor: is a verbal noun and is meant to emphasize the verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although offenders assumed there would be no accounting, God recorded every deed meticulously, leaving no possibility of error or forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: the Almighty had counted each and every deed of theirs by recording it in writing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense makes future punishment vivid; they must taste their deeds, and their condition worsens through increasing torment without respite.
rows.anchor: to make a future event more effective.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous outcome follows the rebels’ fate for contrast; fear of judgment keeps people righteous, while its absence lets Satan overcome them.
rows.anchor: the real thing which keeps a person on the right path is fear of the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥadāʾiq commonly means palm orchards; an ideal orchard has boundary palms and inner vines and crops, with grapes specified after the general image.
rows.anchor: commonly used for orchards of palm-trees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hur are in blooming youth and the same age as Paradise’s inhabitants, supporting closeness, friendship, and companionship.
rows.anchor: For mutual closeness, friendship and association, being of the same age is essential.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise’s brimming pure wine gives delight without intoxication, loss of sense, indecent talk, or lies, unlike worldly wine.
rows.anchor: not affect their senses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly drunkenness can produce false allegations that cause lasting enmity between families and tribes; Arabs strongly valued honor.
rows.anchor: basis of permanent enmity between families and tribes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quranic term kidhdhāban refers to speech and allegations that can besmirch honor with irreparable consequences.
rows.anchor: used by the Qur’ ān refers to such conversation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives believers their due reward, erases none of their pious deeds, and grants more through grace.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will not obliterate the slightest of their pious deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward comes from the sole Lord of all creation; no associate can grant anything on God’s behalf.
rows.anchor: The reward mentioned above is from the Lord of the heavens and earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse denies the idolaters’ claim that their deities can speak to God or intercede; only those permitted may speak truthfully.
rows.anchor: The words refer to the alleged deities of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are worshiped as God’s daughters by idolaters, but Gabriel and other angels stand before God as servants and can only speak by permission and truthfully.
rows.anchor: The verse says that Gabriel and other angels will stand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse rules out the belief that deities can cajole God or intercede as they wish.
rows.anchor: In other words, if the Idolaters wrongly believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-rūḥ means Gabriel, a common Quranic usage; he is named first to show that no other angel has authority, while the alternative “human souls” lacks evidence.
rows.anchor: there is no reason to accept this interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day is certain and cannot be deferred; the warning duty is to inform people and each person should seek a home with the Lord.
rows.anchor: Firstly, the only responsibility of God and His Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God and the Prophet must inform people, not force fear into their hearts; refuge on that Day is with God alone and requires following His path in this life.
rows.anchor: Firstly, the only responsibility of God and His Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one may speak on God’s behalf unless permitted, and only truthfully.
rows.anchor: No one will have even the authority to speak on His behalf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final warning is of imminent worldly punishment under God’s established practice after the Messenger’s arrival, preceding the Hereafter; death brings one’s judgment.
rows.anchor: after the advent of the Messenger of God among these people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day each person sees their deeds; the unprepared despair and wish they had remained dust.
rows.anchor: the deeds of each person will be shown to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh story fits the sūrah’s theme: Moses earnestly called Pharaoh from arrogance, and God destroyed the resistant tyrant with a slight onslaught of wind.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) very earnestly tried to bring the Pharaoh to the right path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Re-creation is easy for the One who made the heavens and earth and arranged night, day, and human sustenance; power enables it and wisdom entails it.
rows.anchor: His power bears witness that He can do so and His wisdom entails that He should do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts the rebellious and disobedient people’s fate with glad tidings for those who feared God.
rows.anchor: A mention of the fate of the rebellious and the disobedient on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not be troubled by demands for the Hour’s timing: only God knows it, the Prophet’s duty is warning, and at its sight people will feel they stayed only a short while.
rows.anchor: The time of arrival of the Day of Judgement is something which only the Almighty knows
